title: Binary Search Trees
explainer_md:
A binary search tree is a binary tree with an ordering invariant: for every node, all values in its left subtree are smaller and all in its right subtree are larger. That invariant means search, insert, and delete each follow a single root-to-leaf path — O(h) time, which is O(log n) when the tree stays balanced.

The single most important BST fact: an **inorder traversal yields the values in sorted order**. A huge fraction of BST problems are solved by exploiting this — validating a BST, finding the k-th smallest, finding the closest value, or spotting a swapped pair all lean on inorder order.

Mental model: a decision tree for 'guess the number' — at each node you go left (smaller) or right (larger), halving the search space when balanced.
patterns_md:
**Ordered navigation** — to find/insert/delete, compare with the current node and go left or right. One path, O(h).

**Inorder = sorted** — leverage it for k-th smallest (inorder and stop at k), validate BST (inorder must be strictly increasing), or find two swapped nodes.

**Range exploitation** — pass down `(low, high)` bounds to validate or to prune search to a value range.

**Balanced-tree awareness** — a naive BST degrades to O(n) if inserted in sorted order. Self-balancing variants (AVL, Red-Black) keep O(log n); `std::set`/`std::map` are Red-Black trees under the hood.
complexity_md:
| Operation | Balanced | Worst (skewed) |
|---|---|---|
| Search | O(log n) | O(n) |
| Insert | O(log n) | O(n) |
| Delete | O(log n) | O(n) |
| Inorder traversal | O(n) | O(n) |
| k-th smallest | O(h + k) | O(n) |

Everything hinges on height. Balanced ⇒ O(log n); a sorted-order insertion sequence makes it a linked list ⇒ O(n).
